prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and of the active incretin peptide that led to a new class of therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the only ballot with first-place support from five of six members and top-three support from all six, but I do not rest the case on that count. The scientific chain runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to receptor pharmacology and drugs that treat type 2 diabetes and obesity and reduce cardiovascular and renal events. It has decades of independent confirmation and very large randomized trials. Maturity is not in doubt. Holst for the physiology, Drucker for the biology and translation, and Mojsov for the active peptide is the scientific discovery core within the three-name cap.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Habener is not among the credited names, the Mojsov-Habener-Holst priority history is contested, and the cap forces Knudsen out, although long-acting analogue design is what made the physiology a therapy. A prize that honours discovery and omits the drug developers could look incomplete, and one that includes Knudsen in place of Mojsov rewards industrial development over the basic finding. Much of my own recollection of the priority history is unverified, so my trio is a judgment about the discovery core and not a settled fact.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked the unfolded protein response (B007) first as a conceptually original and mechanistically complete signalling pathway, and listed GLP-1 third with Knudsen in place of Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree that B007 is a clean two-person discovery (Walter, Mori) and that it is not premature. It is my fallback if the GLP-1 attribution cannot be resolved. On the Mojsov versus Knudsen question I disagree. Knudsen's contribution is real but industrial. Putting her in place of Mojsov, whose work is the identification of the active peptide, would credit the drug and drop the discovery. I would rather settle the attribution on the scientific core than on the product. Perlmann's point about priority disputes is fair, and I accept that it remains open. Disease relevance for the UPR is still largely preclinical, which is why I keep it as an alternative and not my first choice.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supported GLP-1 with Holst, Drucker and Knudsen as a trio spanning physiology to therapeutics, and ranked TNF blockade (B027) third.
responses.response: Her trio is coherent and reflects how the field reached patients, and I take seriously her view that translation should be recognised. I still prefer Mojsov, because the committee's central question is who made the discovery and not who made the product, and the active-peptide identification is a decisive step. We differ here and I do not think the difference is resolved. On B027, TNF blockade is mature and a clean bench-to-bedside story. Its clean two-person credit is a real strength. I do not rank it above GLP-1 or CAR-T on breadth of impact or on the originality of the mechanism, but I would like to hear whether she sees it as competitive with CAR-T.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked optogenetics (B004) second as a transformative general-purpose method that has reached early clinical use in vision restoration, while noting that six credited people exceed the cap.
responses.response: I accept the originality and the scale of its effect on neuroscience, and as a neuroscientist I would not dismiss it. I am not persuaded it should outrank CAR-T or the UPR in this round. Clinical use is early. The credit problem is severe, since any trio leaves out Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, each with a strong claim. A prize for a tool also needs a case that it has conferred benefit on humankind, and that case is currently weaker than for a therapy. My standing in neurology should not tilt this ranking either way.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked GLP-1 first but flagged Mojsov as a decisive yet contested part of the credit with Knudsen as a possible substitute, and proposed a two-person CAR-T credit (June, Sadelain).
responses.response: We largely agree on GLP-1, and I share his caution about the contested part of Mojsov's credit. I would keep Mojsov, but I accept that the committee could reasonably go either way. On CAR-T, I think a two-person credit is more fragile than the three-person version, because Rosenberg's adoptive transfer work is real but adjacent to receptor design, and the original CAR concept (Eshhar and others) is outside the credited names. A two-person prize would sharpen that gap. I would want to resolve it before CAR-T becomes the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third GLP-1 place, and how to weigh Habener's absence from the credited names.
Whether the committee wants to honour physiology and peptide discovery only, or also the drug development that made it a therapy.
Whether CAR-T credit can be allocated fairly when early CAR pioneers are outside the credited names.
Whether UPR (B007) has enough disease-relevant evidence to serve as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I co-authored roughly twenty works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy), a topic unrelated to any shortlisted ballot, and I worked with Paul Greengard, who is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I am a neurologist, which may touch optogenetics (B004) and antisense therapy for SMA (B035) only by field, not by any personal tie.
